newsitem.title: USA: Housing starts rise in April.
newsitem.headline: Housing starts rise in April.

text.p: Construction starts on new homes and apartments rose in April as a burst of building in the South helped boost overall activity, the Commerce Department said on Friday.

Total starts were up 2.6 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.47 million in April after a revised 7.7 percent drop to 1.43 million in March, the department said. Wall Street analysts had forecast April housing starts at a rate of 1.43 million a year.

Construction starts on single-family homes rose 0.3 percent in April to a rate of 1.12 million after falling 9.9 percent in March. Starts on apartments rose 10.9 percent to a rate of 355,000 following a 0.9 percent increase in March.

Mortage rates have been drifting lower since early April. The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp., or Freddie Mac, said rates for a 30-year loan averaged 7.91 percent this week, down from a high of 8.18 percent on April 3.
Total starts during April were 3.2 percent lower than they were a year earlier in April 1996.

Although mortgage rates have declined in recent weeks, builders are concerned that Federal Reserve policymakers will nudge short-term rates up another quarter percentage point when they meet next week, as they did at their last meeting in March.

The National Association of Home Builders said on Thursday that its index of market activity fell in May by two points to a level of 54. The builders cited a slowing market and concern over the prospects that the Fed might nudge interest rates higher, but said the index was still healthy.

"Clearly, builders are concerned about conditions in the market," said Kent Collins, executive vice president of the association. "The market is slowing as we expected and it is likely that the Fed will boost interest rates again when it meets next week."
Interest rates affect not only homebuyers' ability to carry mortgages but also builders' costs to initiate projects.
Starts jumped during April in the South, the nation's biggest regional housing market, by 11.3 percent to an annual rate of 699,000 after a 6.4 percent drop in March.
The April starts level in the South was the highest since July 1995, when starts stood at 728,000, the department said.
In the Midwest, starts climbed 0.7 percent during April to a rate of 292,000 after dropping 24.9 percent in March.

April starts fell 7.4 percent in the Northeast to a rate of 137,000 after a 9.6 percent gain in March. In the West, April starts fell 6.5 percent to 345,000 a year after a 1.9 percent increase in March.
